title: Lokanatha Gosvami
html:
The Seventh Gosvami

Srila Lokanatha Gosvami Prabhu is honoured as an eternal associate of Sri Chaitanya and one of His closest devotees. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in his “Anubhashya” calls him a completely detached associate of Mahaprabhu, a maha-bhagavata and a gosvami. Narottama's songs call him “Prabhu Lokanatha,” the “Karnananda” “Gosani Lokanatha,” and by family he was a Chakravarti, the son of Padmanabha Chakravarti. One of the biographies also regards him as a direct disciple of Mahaprabhu.

Among the Gosvamis of Vrindavana he was the eldest. He was the first of Chaitanya's devotees to come to Vraja, before Rupa and Sanatana, and he lived there so long that by the time of the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” he was the oldest of Mahaprabhu's devotees still remaining in this world; it was to him, already a very old man, that his only disciple Narottama came. Together with his inseparable friend Bhugarbha he is honoured as the seventh Gosvami, after the six Gosvamis of Vrindavana.

Less is known of him than of many other associates of the Lord, and not by chance. He himself forbade Krishnadasa Kaviraja to write about him, and in the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” only his name remains. Everything else was preserved by later books and by the tradition of the Vaishnavas of Vraja.

From Talkhari

Lokanatha was born in the village of Talkhari (Talakhadi) in the district of Yashohar (Jessore) in East Bengal — today Bangladesh. Narahari Chakravarti in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” calls the village Talakhaida. His parents, Padmanabha Chakravarti and Sita Devi, were deeply pious brahmanas:1

“He lived in the village of Talakhaida in the land of Yashohara; his mother was Sita, his father Padmanabha Chakravarti.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.296)

Earlier the family had lived in Kanchrapara.2 Padmanabha was a disciple of Advaita Prabhu and very dear to him; according to one biography, both parents were Advaita's disciples. The “Narottama-vilasa” adds that Padmanabha constantly went to Nadia to see Gauranga, and that Sita dedicated her son to the feet of Gaurachandra.

The “Advaita-prakasha,” a less reliable source, tells more: according to it, Lokanath Chakravarti studied under Advaita together with Gadadhara and Gaura, became learned in the “Bhagavata,” received the Krishna mantra from Advaita, and Advaita entrusted him to Nimai; and Gaura, travelling in East Bengal, visited Padmanabha's house.

On how many children the family had, the sources differ. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” names Lokanatha's only younger brother, Pragalbha; his descendants, the Bhattacharyas of Talakhadi, live there to this day.3 The same note gives the way to Talakhadi: by the Eastern Bengal Railway to Yashohar station, from there by bus to Sonakhali, then to Khejura, and on foot from there — in the rains, by boat.

Childhood

Lokanatha grew up among genuine Vaishnavas, and the signs of a strong love for God showed in him from his earliest years. His sharp mind and rare gift for Sanskrit amazed all who knew him. But learning was not his aim: whenever he heard the names “Krishna,” “Govinda,” “Madhava,” “Hari,” he was lost in them, and tears came to his eyes. His heart was not in worldly affairs, and even living at home he remained detached.

Meanwhile the name of Gauranga spread through the land, and everyone came to know that He is Lord Krishna Himself. The heart of Lokanatha, an eternal associate in whom bhakti was inborn, answered the news. He was irresistibly drawn to Gauranga's feet, and his anxiety grew day by day. From his home to Navadvipa-Mayapura was only two days' walk.

His parents, pious themselves, did not want to let their son go. His mother begged him in tears to give up the idea, but her pleading only strengthened his resolve. Though they were Advaita's disciples and longed to see Gauranga, they never went to Him themselves: they feared that their son, once he met the Lord, would follow Him and never come back. “It is our great good fortune to have such a son,” they said, “but is it pleasing to God that you leave your parents? Serve Him at home.”

At last his parents secretly resolved to marry him, though he was still a boy. One of the biographies calls this a mistake and recalls Raghunatha Dasa: he too was married to a beautiful wife and, when he once ran away, was caught and brought back, yet he could not be held. Learning of the plan, Lokanatha left home at the first opportunity.4

A Night in Agrahayana

He left in the month of Agrahayana (Margashirsha), at the beginning of winter, on a moonlit night: an inner voice was calling him. So he left his parents and his home for ever.5 Heedless of hunger, thirst, fatigue and the roughness of the way, he walked without stopping and by the evening of the next day reached Navadvipa-Mayapura.

On the way he was tormented by doubts: was he destined to see the Lord's feet? Was he, so insignificant, worthy? His only comfort was the thought of the Lord's mercy. In Navadvipa someone, though he had asked nothing, pointed out the Lord's house to him. At the door he could not bring himself to enter: his body grew heavy, his strength and consciousness left him.

With the Lord in Navadvipa

The Lord was sitting among Srivasa, Murari, Mukunda, Haridasa and other devotees. He was told of the newcomer, and at once He came out, embraced the youth with great tenderness and said: “Dear Lokanatha, why did you forget Me for so long? For many days I have been thinking of you.”6

Lokanatha fainted on the Lord's chest. When he came to, he could only weep, clasping His feet: the prayers he had been preparing all the way were never spoken. For several days he remained half-conscious of the outer world, like one dreaming, in bliss he had never known, and all that time the Lord was in his heart.

The Messenger Sent Ahead

One day the Lord said to him: from the time Lokanatha had grown attached to Him, merely by hearing of His name and glories, He had felt deep affection for him; and now it was His wish that Lokanatha should go and live in Vrindavana. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says:

“Prabhu Gaurachandra showed him great mercy and ordered him to go to Vrindavana quickly. Such an order was not without purpose: the Lord was soon going to accept sannyasa. Having become a sannyasi He would go to Vrindavana — that is why He wished to send him ahead.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.300–302)

Gently as it was spoken, the order struck Lokanatha like lightning. Why should the Lord send him away while others stayed with Him? He pleaded that he not be sent where His sankirtana and His sweet words could not be heard.

The Lord answered tenderly that separation was hard for Him too. Now it was Agrahayana, then would come Pausha, and in Magha He would accept sannyasa. Let Lokanatha go before Him as His messenger and await Him at Chira-ghata in Vrindavana: He would come there, and other Vaishnavas would come too. Meanwhile the lost places of Krishna's pastimes should, as far as possible, be found and restored; the wait would not be long.

According to one biography, it was Lokanatha who first learned of the Lord's coming sannyasa — before even Nityananda, His second self.7 This shows how dear and beloved he was to the Lord.

According to the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” the Lord did not name the time directly: Lokanatha understood from His hints that in a day or two the Lord would accept sannyasa.8 He pictured the Lord without His beautiful curls, pictured the grief of the devotees — and wept:

“‘His beautiful curling hair will be seen no more — how will those who love Him keep their lives?’ At these thoughts alone he was thrown into turmoil and, weeping, bowed at the Lord's feet.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.304–305)

But he did not dare disobey. Laying his head on the Lord's feet, he bathed them with tears, joyfully accepted the order and asked to be shown what he should do. He surrendered himself completely to the Lord. The Lord embraced him — and every place of the Vrindavana pastimes opened within Lokanatha's heart. The Lord told him to perform bhajana at Chira-ghata, beneath a dense canopy of kadamba, bakula and tamala, and comforted him with instructions: “We shall meet in Vrindavana.”

“The all-knowing Lord embraced Lokanatha, secretly comforted him and sent him off. Lokanatha gave himself to the Lord's feet, bowed to the Lord's associates and departed.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.306–307)

The “Prema-vilasa,” a less reliable source, says that in that secret conversation the Lord revealed to Lokanatha the bhava of Radha and the reason for His sannyasa. He told him to live at Chira-ghata, at Rasa-sthali and Nidhuvana, and to instruct people: “I have given you My own land, Vrindavana, as a gift.”

The next morning Bhugarbha, a disciple of Gadadhara Pandita, set out with Lokanatha: Gadadhara let him go, and the Lord looked on them with approval. Thus these two became the first of Chaitanya's devotees to leave for Vrindavana; Lokanatha was the first of the Gaudiya Vaishnavas to be sent there by the Lord.9 How this came about is told in more detail in the article on Bhugarbha.

To Vraja

For about two months the friends walked, without money, living on alms: through Rajmahal, Tejpur, Purnia, Ayodhya, Lucknow and Agra. Vraja met them with desolation: the holy places were overgrown with forest and forgotten. For a long time they could not find Chira-ghata with its Kadamba-kunja, nor Vamshivata, Shyama-kunda or Radha-kunda; they wept and called to Radha and Krishna, as if mad with love. The “Prema-vilasa” says that by the Lord's power Lokanatha recognised the places of His pastimes.

Searching for the Lord

Meanwhile the Lord accepted sannyasa and went south, where He travelled for two years, and then came to Vrindavana.10 But Lokanatha was not there. According to one biography, on hearing of the Lord's journey south, he and Bhugarbha — Lokanatha above all — went south to find Him, and so for the whole two months that the Lord spent in Vraja they were away.

The “Bhakti-ratnakara” tells of the search thus: after sannyasa the Lord came to Nilachala and from there set out to travel in the South — and Lokanatha, hearing of it, went south; from the South the Lord came to Vrindavana — and Lokanatha went to Vraja; but from Vrindavana the Lord went on to Prayaga, and Lokanatha, reaching Vraja, was in despair:

“He resolved to set out for Prayaga in the morning, but in a dream the Lord comforted him and kept him in Vrindavana. Lokanatha could not transgress the Lord's command and lived unknown in the forests of Vraja.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.313–314)11

What the Lord said in that dream is told in different ways. According to one biography, He said: “Had we met, you would have grieved to see Me in the dress of a sannyasi. Behold Me rather in My former form, with My beautiful curls.” Then Lokanatha understood why they had missed each other: the Lord was sparing his love, for the mere thought of the Lord in sannyasa dress, a blanket on His shoulders, caused him great pain. According to another biography, the Lord told him to stop wandering and remain in Vrindavana for bhajana. According to a third, the Lord said: “Lokanatha, stay in Vrindavana. I have not broken My word: I have come to Vrindavana and live here in another form; so you will always be with Me.” The Lord is non-different from Krishna, and Vrindavana is His eternal abode; His promise “I shall come” He fulfilled. The “Narottama-vilasa” speaks of two dreams: in one Lokanatha saw the young Gaura in Navadvipa, in the other the Lord as a sannyasi, and the Lord foretold to him a disciple — Narottama.

Comforted, Lokanatha gave up the hope of seeing the Lord and resolved to carry out His order. Together with Bhugarbha he found the Kadamba-kunja and Chira-ghata, and there the friends remained for the remainder of their days. Day and night they sang the names of Krishna, leaving only an hour or two for rest and sleep, and kept far from people.

Among the Gosvamis of Vrindavana

Soon the Lord's associates began to come to Vraja — Rupa, Sanatana, Gopala Bhatta and others — and their company brought Lokanatha immense joy. All of them were one in mind and heart, and the love they exchanged was wonderful. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says:

“After some time he met Rupa and Sanatana — what joy in Vrindavana! Sri Gopala Bhatta and all the other associates of the Lord — who can tell how close he was to them all?” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.315–316)

There too Narahari Chakravarti says that for some time Lokanatha served Sri Govinda and the other Deities, ever overwhelmed with prema — the very limit of renunciation.12 In the mangalacharanas of the first waves of the “Bhakti-ratnakara” Narahari glorifies Lokanatha and Bhugarbha, full of prema, and he describes Gopala Bhatta in the company of Lokanatha, Bhugarbha, Kashishvara and others.

In the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” Lokanatha's name occurs only once. When Gopala, on the pretext of fear of the Muslims, came from Govardhana to Mathura, to the house of Vitthaleshvara — in truth out of mercy for the aged Rupa — Rupa spent a whole month there beholding Him, and his associates were with him:

“Then Rupa Gosani took all his associates with him, stayed in Mathura for a month and had darshana of Gopala. With him were Gopala Bhatta, Raghunatha Dasa, Raghunatha Bhatta Gosani and Lokanatha…” (CC, Madhya 18.48–49)13

Sanatana Gosvami named him in his books to invoke blessings, and Narahari Chakravarti quotes both verses. In the mangalacharana of the “Hari-bhakti-vilasa” (1.4) it is said:

“Kashishvara shines in Krishna's forest, and so does Sri Krishnadasa with Lokanatha.”

And at the beginning of the “Vaishnava-toshani,” the commentary on the Tenth Canto of the “Bhagavata”:

“I praise those dear to Vrindavana, who have taken shelter at Sri Govinda's feet: the illustrious Kashishvara, Lokanatha and Sri Krishnadasa.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.321, 1.323)14

Closest of all to him was Bhugarbha:

“His affection for Bhugarbha is known to the world: only their bodies were different from Lokanatha's.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.317)

And in the sixth wave of the same book Narahari says that Gopala Bhatta is most merciful, and Bhugarbha and Lokanatha are a mine of virtues.15 And in the “Namamrita-samudra,” his prayers to the Lord's associates, Narahari calls upon the two together:

“O Sri Bhugarbha, Lokanatha! Take pity this once — there is no one as fallen as I.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 27)

He was close to Gopala Bhatta as well. Manohara Dasa, in a song about Gopala Bhatta, calls him, Pandita Krishna and Lokanatha one soul in different bodies, and a song of Narahari says that Lokanatha would meet Gopala Bhatta in the assembly of devotees, and that Gopala Bhatta lived now in Gokula-Mahavana, now near his dear Lokanatha. And when the Lord sent Gopala Bhatta His waist-cord and seat, Bhugarbha and Lokanatha, according to the “Prema-vilasa,” fell to the ground at the sight of them.

He also stayed at Radha-kunda, where Raghunatha Dasa had settled. The “Karnananda” relates:

“With him were Krishnadasa and Lokanatha Gosani; day and night — unceasing talk of Krishna. At that time the book called ‘Gopala-champu’ they all relished together unceasingly.” (“Karnananda” 4.432–433)

According to the same book, Raghunatha Dasa vowed to leave his body before the eyes of Jiva, Krishnadasa and Lokanatha; and when Srinivasa was receiving blessings for his journey, Lokanatha and Bhugarbha prayed to Govinda for him.

And yet Lokanatha and Bhugarbha stood apart from what made the six Gosvamis famous. They displayed the pastime of “maha-vivikta bhajanandis” — the most secluded devotees, whose bliss lies in bhajana; they wrote no books and did not preach, and so were not counted among the “six.” Lokanatha, a viviktanandi worshipping the Lord in solitude, set the example of bhajana in renunciation within the dhama itself. Vrindavana Dasa in the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” names neither him nor Bhugarbha — perhaps because of their own prohibition, but in no way from any ill will; nor is his name found in Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's “Gaudiya-bhashya.”

Radha-vinoda

Lokanatha constantly wandered through Vraja, visiting the places of Krishna's pastimes in ecstasy — he went round all twelve forests and stayed in Khadiravana. Near Chhatravana, by the village of Umrao, lies Kishori-kunda, dear to Radha. The place captivated him, and he stayed there for solitary bhajana, at times living right in the forest.

For long years he was absorbed in nama-bhajana, and at last an ardent desire arose in his heart to serve Radha and Krishna in the form of the Deity. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” tells how the Lord answered that desire:

“The Lord knew that Lokanatha was yearning, and came in another form, bringing a Deity. Telling Him His name — Radha-vinoda — He handed Him over and at that very moment vanished from there.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.327–328)16

Lokanatha was amazed, and then troubled: who had given him such a Deity, and where had the giver gone? Could it have been the Lord Himself who came and went? Then Radha-vinoda looked at him sweetly, smiled and spoke:

“‘I live in the forest by this village of Umrao; here, at this Kishori-kunda, is My place. Seeing your longing, I too grew restless: who will bring Me? — and I came Myself. Quickly give Me something to eat.’” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.331–333)17

Shedding tears of love, Lokanatha quickly prepared food, and Radha-vinoda ate with pleasure — fine rice on a fresh banana leaf. Lokanatha made Him a bed of flowers, fanned Him with leafy branches and joyfully pressed His feet. From that day he gave body, mind and life to Radha-vinoda and drank the nectar of His beauty. The “Narottama-vilasa” says that, looking at Radha-vinoda, Lokanatha saw in Him the beauty of Gaura and wept that he had not seen His pastimes.

Lokanatha had no home and did not know where to keep the Deity. So he sewed a large bag, and it became Radha-vinoda's temple: he wore it round his neck and kept the Lord against his heart as a precious necklace. So it was to the end of his days — an example of strict vairagya. According to one biography, the bag was a blanket hung from his neck, and in the rain Lokanatha set Radha-vinoda inside a hollow tree and was himself drenched, as before. He lived under a tree, in rain and cold, keeping the vow of ayachaka — never asking anyone for food.

Seeing his love for the Lord, the villagers and cowherds of Vraja wanted to build him a hut, but he refused: nothing pleased him but a place among the roots of trees. So great was his renunciation that he took only the barest necessities.18 After living at the kunda, he came to Vrindavana, where all the Gosvamis lovingly kept him among them, and he always cherished their company.

His beloved Radha-vinoda receives service in Vrindavana to this day, in the temple of Radha-Gokulananda.

“Let Not Even a Stone Tell Where I Lie”

All his life Lokanatha fled from honour. He thought himself unworthy of being called a saint and shunned every mark of respect; he stayed alone, except for the hours when Vaishnavas came to him or gathered for sankirtana. Worshipping Radha and Krishna in the deep mood of separation, he grew ever more detached and fled from the least fame.

When Krishnadasa Kaviraja, who took up the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” at the wish of the Vraja Gosvamis, approached Lokanatha for his blessing even before beginning the work, Lokanatha blessed him but set a condition: nowhere in the book was he to mention his name, his deeds or his way of life. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains in the “Anubhashya”: probably out of great humility. Narahari Chakravarti speaks of the same prohibition by Gopala Bhatta, who considered himself the lowest of all, and adds:

“Lokanatha Gosvami too gave such an order; this I heard from the lips of old Vaishnavas.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.225)

This is not worldly modesty or concern for a good name, but the humility of a pure devotee — amani, one who seeks no honour for himself. Kaviraja remembered the condition and kept it: Lokanatha's name stands in his book only in a single list, and of his renunciation and bhakti there is not a word. That is why his name is so rarely met in the “Chaitanya-charitamrita.” Nor are Srinivasa and Narottama, Lokanatha's disciple, named there — something many people ask about.

To him, as to no one else, applies the saying: “Let not even a stone tell where I lie.” Lokanatha and the few devotees of Mahaprabhu like him effaced the memory of themselves. As long as even a shadow of desire for fame remains in the heart, bhajana is impossible.

Narottama, the Only Disciple

Lokanatha did not accept disciples: such was his vow. He made an exception for one alone — Narottama. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Anubhashya” that he gave initiation to Narottama Thakura Mahashaya alone, and the shastras make no mention of any other disciple of his; the “Prema-vilasa” calls him the first among the renounced, and Narottama his servant. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says:

“On the full moon of the month of Shravana, at an auspicious moment, Lokanatha accepted Narottama as his disciple.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.294)

Narottama, the son of Raja Krishnananda Datta of Gopalpura in Rajshahi, left his home at the Karttika full moon, visited many tirthas and came to Vrindavana. This was after Rupa and Sanatana had passed from sight. Lokanatha could not bear the separation: day and night he wept for them, life stayed in him only by the Lord's will, and the one aim of his life became to fulfil the Lord's desires. It was then that Narottama came to him.19

Jiva Gosvami sent the youth to serve Lokanatha's feet. Lokanatha was by then very old, and so tormented by separation from Gauranga that it seemed life had left him. When Narottama bowed to him, he asked: “Who are you?” — “Your fallen servant. I wish to serve your feet.” — “How can I accept anyone's service, when I myself do not know how to serve Gaura and Nityananda?” But Narottama had vowed to accept initiation from Lokanatha alone. The “Narottama-vilasa” says that Lokanatha recognised in him the disciple whom the Lord had foretold to him in a dream, and the “Prema-vilasa,” that Rupa in a dream told Jiva to entrust the youth to Lokanatha, and that Lokanatha, who had also seen him in a dream, brought Narottama back to consciousness with the touch of his hand when he had fainted at the Govinda temple.

Narottama was drawn by Lokanatha's austere renunciation. He began to serve him in secret. Every night he cleaned the place where Lokanatha went to relieve himself. Surprised at its cleanliness, Lokanatha one night hid in the bushes, chanting japa all night, and at midnight caught the raja's son at his cleaning. He was embarrassed — not from pride but from humility: it seemed to him an offence that a Vaishnava, a raja's son, should secretly serve him — and he asked why he was doing this and told him to stop. Narottama fell weeping at his feet: “Without your mercy my life is useless.” The “Prema-vilasa” adds details: Narottama sifted earth so that his guru would have something to clean his hands with, brought water, hid the broom of coconut-palm leaves and, pressing it to his chest, wept: “Here I shall gain the strength to reach the feet of my master.”

This service lasted about a year. Seeing Narottama's humility and his anguish, Lokanatha softened his resolve and gave him the mantras of initiation. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says it briefly:

“At that very time Narottama came there and joyfully served his guru as is fitting. Pleased with his service, he gave him the mantra of initiation and showed Narottama boundless mercy.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.345–346)

The song of Vasanta, which Narahari quotes a little further on, says the same: Narottama, renouncing royal pleasures, “gave himself to the feet of Prabhu Lokanatha” in Vrindavana, and “Lokanatha mercifully accepted him as his own” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.418–419).

According to the “Prema-vilasa,” before initiation Narottama chanted Hari-nama for a year, and Lokanatha set him conditions: not to marry, not to eat fish or parboiled rice. He taught that Krishna appears in the form of the guru, that for a year the disciple observes the guru and the guru tests the disciple, and that the Gosvamis do not bid one accept many disciples. The secret service, according to this book, lasted a year, and Narottama was initiated in the month of Vaishakha (according to the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” on the full moon of Shravana). There too Lokanatha reveals to Narottama his eternal name — Vilasa-manjari — and instructs him in sadhana.

Narottama's story shows how honest, selfless service wins the guru's heart. This is no “menial work” but the exemplary service of a disciple, and unwavering devotion to the guru is the chief mark of a disciple. Lokanatha and Narottama displayed this pastime to the world, especially to North Bengal. So too Srila Gaurakishora Dasa Babaji, who had vowed not to accept disciples, long refused Srila Bhaktisiddhanta but yielded before his humility and accepted him as his only disciple. Secluded bhajanandis do not themselves build communities, but, bound by the service of their one disciple, they give rise to a community through him.

Lokanatha saw in Narottama not only a noble upbringing but also zeal and a taste for being among people. His former position as a wealthy zamindar made Narottama especially fit for preaching in North Bengal: there he could teach people a renounced life. And Lokanatha, out of compassion, told him to return to his homeland, to Kheturi, and preach Krishna consciousness. Secluded viviktanandis are usually not inclined to works for people's welfare, but when a devotee of Narottama's stature takes them up, those works themselves are elevated; Lokanatha instructed the world through his disciple — as a mother-in-law teaches the daughter-in-law while instructing her own daughter.

Srinivasa knew Lokanatha's intention. When the books of the Gosvamis were stolen on the way to Gauda, he told Narottama: “Go quickly to Kheturi and carry out Lokanatha's order” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 7.119). So, by his guru's will, Narottama left Vrindavana. The “Prema-vilasa” tells also of Lokanatha's instructions before his departure and of his weeping at the news of the theft of the books.

What he entrusted to his disciple the “Bhakti-ratnakara” tells thus:

“When Narottama came to Gauda, Prabhu Lokanatha gave the command: the service of the Deities of Sri Gauranga and Krishna, service to the Sri Vaishnavas, and the Lord's sankirtana. As he was commanded, so he applied himself: he established the service of six beautiful Deities.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.422–424)

The six Deities of Kheturi — Gauranga, Vallavikanta, Vrajamohana, Sri Krishna, Radha-kanta and Radha-ramana — were manifested at Lokanatha's command; and at his command too Shyamananda was invited to the festival at Kheturi.

Narottama remembered his guru all his life. In the songs of the “Prarthana” he prays that Prabhu Lokanatha take him along and give him to the feet of Sri Rupa; he laments over the rope of mercy by which the Lord drew him to Vraja and which, as he humbly says, maya and fate cut through; he cries “ha ha prabhu lokanatha”: without his mercy one attains neither Chaitanya nor Radha and Krishna. And in a humble song about the Gosvamis whom, as he says, he never served, he names Lokanatha among them.

Later, in Navadvipa, Narottama told how in Vrindavana he had lived in the care of Jiva and Lokanatha; and in Khardaha Jahnava and Vasudha, seeing that the mercy of Lokanatha and Jiva was upon him, bestowed their own mercy on him as well. The “Prema-vilasa” tells that Lokanatha and Jiva wept with joy at news from Kheturi and sent Vaishnavas there with messages, and that Lokanatha told Narottama to beware of offences.

From Mahaprabhu through Lokanatha runs Narottama's diksha line, to which Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura also belonged: Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu — Lokanatha Gosvami — Narottama — Ganganarayana Chakravarti — Krishnacharana — Radharamana — Vishvanatha. In Vishvanatha's verse on his guru-line Lokanatha is named as the one whose guru is Gauranga Himself; and Vishvanatha writes his “Sankalpa-kalpadruma” under the guidance of Sri Lokanatha and Sri Narottama, and among his minor works is an eight-verse hymn in Lokanatha's honour, the “Sri Lokanathashtaka.” For Lokanatha the Lord was his Lord and teacher: He accepted him, instructed him and sent him to Vraja. How his initiation took place the sources do not describe.20

Srinivasa, Jahnava, Ramachandra

When Srinivasa came to Vrindavana, Jiva Gosvami presented him to Lokanatha and Bhugarbha:

“Srinivasa bowed at the feet of both, and both embraced him with great tenderness. In loving rapture they could not let him out of their arms and bathed Srinivasa in tears. They entrusted him to the lotus feet of Sri Radha-vinoda.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.357–359)

Before leaving for Gauda with the books of the Gosvamis, Srinivasa, Narottama and Shyamananda received Lokanatha's blessing; according to the “Karnananda,” he was among those who blessed Srinivasa, and according to the “Narottama-vilasa,” he entrusted Narottama to Srinivasa. The second time Srinivasa came to Vrindavana he was in grief, and Lokanatha together with the other elders told him of Gaura and Krishna and consoled him.

When Jahnava Devi came to Vraja, Lokanatha went out with the heads of the Vaishnava community to honour her;21 and at her departure, according to the “Narottama-vilasa,” he blessed Srinivasa and Narottama. According to the “Prema-vilasa,” Jahnava praised Lokanatha's disciple Narottama to him, and on her return brought Lokanatha's blessing to Narottama in Kheturi.

Ramachandra Kaviraja, coming to Vrindavana, was granted the darshana of Lokanatha's feet and received his mercy.22 And of Govinda Kaviraja, Ramachandra's younger brother, the “Bhakti-ratnakara” says that Jiva, Lokanatha and the others in Vrindavana drank the nectar of his songs and together gave him the title of Kaviraja.

Departure

Lokanatha Gosvami left this world in deep old age. By our calendar (Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math) the day of his departure is the krishna-ashtami of the month of Shridhara (in 2026, 6 August); the day of his appearance is not in the calendar, and the sources do not give it.23

According to one biography, he entered the Lord's eternal unmanifest pastimes in Khadiravana, near the village of Khayara, where he was performing bhajana; there lies Yugala-kunda, and on its bank is his samadhi. According to another, his samadhi is in Vrindavana, in the temple of Radha-Gokulananda, where his Radha-vinoda too receives service.

Lila-manjari

Who Lokanatha is in Krishna's eternal pastimes Kavi Karnapura reveals in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika”:

“The former name of Bhugarbha Thakura is Prema-manjari; Lokanatha Gosvami is the former Sri Lila-manjari.” (GGD 187)

In Vraja he is Lila-manjari, a maidservant of Srimati Radharani, and in the same verse his inseparable friend is named beside him.24

The Vaishnavas of old, as Narahari Chakravarti tells, worshipped him thus:

“I worship Sri Lokanatha Prabhu, the son of Padmanabha, possessed of the wealth of the service of Sri Radha-vinoda alone.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.297)25

His whole life is in these words. The first whom the Lord sent to Vraja, he found Radha-vinoda there and served Him to the end; he fled from fame so that even the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” kept only his name; and through his one disciple, Narottama, he founded the line of disciples that descends from Narottama. He is counted among the great souls, full of separation, who relish the hidden pastimes of service, and his renunciation is of one nature with that of Srila Gaurakishora.
